The plan phases around her menstrual cycle, accommodates flow-day restrictions (no high-intensity, no heavy Valsalva, no jumping), and progressively builds strength while prioritizing recovery. Starts on 2026-06-01.

Assumptions and structure
- Cycle days: Day 1 = first day of menses. Flow days 1–3 are the most restrictive.
- Week 1 in the plan corresponds to 2026-06-01, with a rough cycle mapping:
  - Menstrual phase: Days 1–3 flow days; days 4–5 mild symptoms possible; day 6–10 approx. 1st post-flow week.
  - Follicular phase: days 11–14 (roughly after flow), increasing energy and pain-free tolerance.
  - Ovulatory/early luteal: days 15–19.
  - Late luteal: days 20–28 (pre-menstrual symptoms may re-emerge; adjust intensity as needed).
- Session design:
  - Flow days (roughly days 1–3): non-high-intensity, no maximal loads, more technique focus, lighter total volume, controlled tempo, more mobility and core stability.
  - Outside flow window: standard resistance training intensity.
- Weekly cadence: 4 training days per week (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat) with optional 5th recovery or mobility day if needed. If competition or schedule requires, adapt to 3–4 days.

12-week plan overview by phase
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): Foundation and cycle-aware adaptation. Emphasize technique, light loads during flow days, establish consistency, start gradual adaptations.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): Strength foundation and volume increase. Increase load outside flow days; maintain safe, non-Valsalva technique during flow days.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): Strength progression with power-influenced work and autoregulation. Introduce occasional higher intensity on non-flow days.
- Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): Peaking and deload to close cycle. Target 1–2 rep max-ish efforts on non-flow days with controlled technique, finish with deload and performance testing.

Detailed week-by-week plan
Notes for all weeks
- Warm-up: 8–12 minutes including light cardio (bike or treadmill), dynamic mobility for hips, shoulders, and thoracic spine, and warm-up sets for main lifts.
- Core and mobility: 6–10 minutes of core stability and hip/ankle mobility at end of each session.
- Progression: aim to increase load week-to-week by 2.5–5% where tolerable; if form or fatigue limits, hold or decrease.
- Rest between sets: 60–90 seconds for most exercises; 2–3 minutes for heavier compound work as needed.
- Tempo: 2-0-1-1 (two seconds eccentric, no pause, one second concentric, one-second pause) for control during flow days; on non-flow days tempos can be 2-0-1-1 or 1-0-1-1 depending on load.
- Nutrition basics: Protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day; aim for 20–40 g protein per meal; consider anti-inflammatory foods; hydrate well. On heavy days, ensure adequate calories especially around workouts. Consider iron status if symptoms worsen; discuss with GP if heavy bleeding or fatigue persists.

Phase 1: Foundation and cycle-aware adaptation (Weeks 1–3)
Week 1 (2026-06-01 to 2026-06-07)

  - Expense: 3x per week non-high-intensity, technique focus.

- All sessions lower volume and intensity by 40–60%
- Flow days: 2 light technique sessions
- Non-flow days: 2 sessions with light weights and more mobility
- Focus on sleep, nutrition, and recovery

- Re-test 1RM or estimated 1RM for squat, bench, and deadlift (choose 1–2 lifts to test depending on readiness)
- Flow days: recovery-focused, technique work
- Non-flow days: testing blocks if ready
- End with 1-week taper to begin new training cycle

Nutrition and recovery guidance
- Protein target: 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day, distributed across 3–4 meals; include a protein-rich snack post-workout.
- Carbohydrates: maintain energy for training; adjust intake around heavier days to support performance and recovery.
- Fats: keep within general guidelines; emphasize omega-3s (fish, flaxseed) and monounsaturated fats.
- Iron status: particularly relevant with dysmenorrhea; include iron-rich foods (red meat, lentils, spinach, fortified cereals) and monitor fatigue; consult GP if heavy periods persist.
- Hydration: target 30–40 ml/kg/day, more on training days.
- Sleep: aim for 7–9 hours; consider a 20–30 minute post-training mobility or light activity window on recovery days.
- Flow days: avoid heavy Valsalva, no jumping; if abdominal cramps are severe, reduce volume further and focus on diaphragmatic breathing and gentle mobility.

- Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE): track after each set; if RPE exceeds 8/10 for more than two sessions in a week on flow days, drop volume.
- Pain and symptoms: track dysmenorrhea severity and fatigue; adjust flow-day loads accordingly.
- Check-ins: weekly quick check-in on energy, sleep, and mood to adjust upcoming week.

Adaptations and safety
- If flow-day symptoms intensify, substitute with immobilization or mobility day and reduce mechanical loading. If pain or dizziness occurs, stop and reassess with a lighter day or rest.
- If any new medical concerns arise (e.g., heavy menstrual bleeding, unusual fatigue, joint pain), adjust and consult with healthcare providers.

Great idea to bolster cycle-related fatigue and cramps with targeted nutrition. Below is a practical, evidence-informed nutrition plan you can weave into the 12-week program. It covers daily energy, macronutrient targets, micronutrients relevant to dysmenorrhea and energy, hydration, meal timing around training, and specific strategies for flow days vs. non-flow days. It’s written to be actionable for a trainer to hand to the client or modify in your programming.

1) Daily energy and macronutrient targets
- Estimated daily calories: Start with maintenance plus a modest surplus on higher-volume training days to support performance and recovery. For a recreational lifter around this age and activity level, a starting estimate is 28–32 kcal/kg/day, adjusted by weekly weight checks and energy levels.
- Protein: 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day. Distribute across 3–4 meals with ~25–40 g protein per meal.
- Carbohydrates: 3–5 g/kg/day depending on training load and menstrual phase. Higher on heavy training days, lower on light flow days if appetite is reduced.
- Fats: 0.8–1.2 g/kg/day. Include sources of omega-3s and ample fat for hormonal health and satiety.
- Fiber: 25–38 g/day to support GI comfort and gut health; hydrate with fluids to reduce cramping-associated discomfort.

2) Key micronutrients linked to dysmenorrhea and fatigue
- Magnesium (300–420 mg/day elemental): supports muscle relaxation and may help cramping. Sources: pumpkin seeds, almonds, spinach; consider a 150–300 mg elemental magnesium supplement if dietary intake is low (check tolerability; start with glycinate or citrate forms to reduce laxative effect).
- Vitamin B6 (1.3–2.0 mg/day, higher if using fortified foods): supports mood and energy metabolism. Sources: poultry, bananas, potatoes, chickpeas.
- Vitamin B12 and folate: support energy and red blood cell formation. Sources: fortified cereals, meat, dairy, leafy greens.
- Iron: especially important with dysmenorrhea and potential heavy flow. Target: 8–18 mg/day depending on status. Food sources: red meat, poultry, beans, fortified cereals. Consider iron status testing if fatigue persists; iron supplements only under clinician guidance.
- Calcium and Vitamin D: calcium supports muscle function; vitamin D supports immune function and mood. Sources: dairy or fortified alternatives, leafy greens, fatty fish; sunlight exposure or supplementation if deficient.
- Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA): anti-inflammatory; aim for 1–2 servings of fatty fish weekly or 1–2 g/day of combined EPA+DHA via supplement if diet is low in fish.
- Electrolytes: adequate sodium on training days, especially with sweat losses; include electrolyte-containing beverages if workouts are long or hot.

3) Hydration strategy
- Baseline: 30–40 ml/kg/day of fluids.
- During training: 600–1000 ml/hour if sessions exceed 60 minutes; adjust for heat.
- Flow days: increase fluids to help reduce cramping and fatigue; consider a warm beverage or tea to aid comfort.
- Include a hydration plan that includes electrolytes (sodium 300–700 mg per liter, potassium ~200–350 mg per liter) on longer or sweaty sessions.

4) Flow-day considerations (days 1–3)
- Energy intake: mild reduction is okay if appetite is low, but avoid severe energy deficits. Prioritize nourishing, easily digestible meals.
- Pre-activity: keep snacks light and non-gassy; options include a banana with peanut butter, yogurt with berries, or a small smoothie with whey or plant-based protein, 60–90 minutes pre-session if tolerable.
- Training-day adjustments: emphasize technique and lighter carbohydrates around workouts to maintain energy without GI distress. Post-workout: prioritize protein and simple carbs (e.g., chocolate milk, smoothie with whey, fruit) to aid recovery.
- Cramp relief meals: include a small snack containing magnesium-rich foods (e.g., a handful of almonds or a small yogurt with seeds) around the mid-day period to help with cramps.

5) Non-flow day nutrition (days with higher training tolerance)
- Emphasize nutrient timing around heavier sessions:
  - Pre-workout meal: 1–2 hours before with 25–40 g protein and 40–60 g carbs (e.g., oats with whey and berries, rice bowl with chicken).
  - Post-workout: protein + 1.0–1.5 g/kg/day total carbs in the 2–4 hours after training to maximize glycogen replenishment (e.g., rice, potatoes, fruit, yogurt).
- Balanced meals: aim for 0.3–0.5 g fat per kg per meal if fat-sensitive during heavy training days, while ensuring enough calories.

6) Sample daily templates
- Flow-day day (first few days):
  - Breakfast: Greek yogurt parfait with berries, granola, and chia seeds; coffee or tea.
  - Snack: Banana and a handful of almonds.
  - Lunch: Quinoa bowl with grilled chicken, mixed veggies, olive oil dressing; orange.
  - Snack: Hummus with carrot sticks; apple.
  - Dinner: Salmon, sweet potato, and steamed broccoli with a side salad.
  - Optional: small magnesium-rich snack before bed (e.g., a small yogurt with seeds) if cramps are persistent.
- Non-flow day with training:
  - Pre-workout: Oatmeal with whey protein, peanut butter, and banana.
  - Post-workout: Protein smoothie with milk, whey, berries, and a sprinkle of oats.
  - Dinner: Lean steak or tofu stir-fry with brown rice and mixed vegetables.
  - Snacks as needed: cheese and crackers, or a protein-rich yogurt.

7) Supplement guidance (optional and to be discussed with the client)
- Magnesium glycinate or citrate 150–300 mg in the evening (start low to assess tolerance).
- Vitamin D if deficient (based on blood test or local guidelines) at 1000–2000 IU/day; adjust as needed.
- Iron supplementation only if iron status is low or ferritin is under recommended threshold (consult a clinician).
- Omega-3 supplement (1–2 g/day of combined EPA and DHA) if dietary intake is insufficient.
- Consider a B-complex or multivitamin if daily intake of micronutrients is consistently low.

8) Periodization alignment
- On Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): emphasize protein intake around 1.8–2.0 g/kg/day with adequate carb intake to support adaptation and recovery, maintain hydration, and monitor GI tolerance with higher training loads.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): push calories slightly higher on heavy training days; maintain protein at 1.8–2.0 g/kg/day; increase fiber with whole foods to sustain satiety.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): maintain or slightly increase calories if fatigue is persistent; ensure iron and magnesium targets are met; consider larger pre-/post-workout meals on heavier days.
- Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12) and deload: reduce overall intake slightly if training volume drops, but keep protein high to preserve lean mass; maintain hydration and micronutrient sufficiency.

9) Practical implementation tips for you as the trainer
- Use weekly check-ins to adjust calories and macros based on weight trends, energy, and menstrual symptoms.
- Keep a simple food log aligned with training days to monitor patterns and prevent underfueling.
- If appetite declines during flow days, still aim for 3 meals with protein and include a small snack rich in magnesium and potassium to help cramps (e.g., yogurt with seeds, smoothie with spinach and kiwi).
- Consider a meal-prep plan to ensure easy access to high-protein options during flow days when energy is low.

It’s written as a trainer-facing plan with week-by-week structure, including daily session blocks you can copy into a calendar or worksheet.

Assumptions and cycle mapping
- Cycle: 28-day cycle. Day 1 = first day of menses. Flow days = days 1–3.
- Flow-day restrictions: no high-intensity, no heavy Valsalva, no jumping. Emphasize technique, mobility, light loads.
- Outside flow days: standard resistance training with progressive overload, autoregulation as needed.
- Training days: four lifting days per week (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat) with optional cardio days or mobility days as needed. Cardio/conditioning is integrated and adjusted by phase.
- Start date: 2026-06-01. Weeks 1–12 align to calendar weeks with a rough cycle mapping.

Phase structure and week-by-week overview
- Phase 1: Foundation and cycle-aware adaptation (Weeks 1–3)
  - Focus: technique, establish consistency, light loads during flow days, gradual adaptation.
- Phase 2: Strength foundation with increased intensity and volume (Weeks 4–6)
  - Focus: higher loading on non-flow days, clearer progression targets, add plyometric/power day and HIIT day starting Week 4/Week 4–7.
- Phase 3: Strength progression and capacity (Weeks 7–9)
  - Focus: higher intensities on non-flow days; planned 1RM testing window at end of Week 9 if appropriate and symptoms allow.
- Phase 4: Peaking and deload (Weeks 10–12)
  - Focus: tapering, performance testing (optional), deload, and plan reset for next cycle.

Strength plan details (lift structure, sets, reps, tempo)
- General tempo: Flow days use 2-0-1-1 (eccentric 2s, minimal pause, concentric 1s, 1s pause). Non-flow days use 2-0-1-1 or 1-0-1-1 depending on load.
- Rest: 60–90 seconds between sets; 2–3 minutes for heavy main lifts as needed.
- Progression: 2.5–5% load progression weekly if technique and recovery allow.

  - Session B (Thu) Flow:
    - Split squats 3x10 per leg
    - Incline dumbbell press 3x10
    - Hip hinge pattern (good mornings) 3x12
    - Lat pulldown 3x10
    - Farmers carry 3x30–40m
- Non-flow days (Tue, Sat)

    - Seated rows 3x10

  - Session A: Goblet squat 3x12; DB bench/push-up 3x12; RDL 3x12; Row 3x12; Pallof press 3x12; Plank 3x40s

Phase 2: Strength foundation and volume increase (Weeks 4–6)
Phase 2 baseline note: Flow-day loads stay light; non-flow days push heavier loading with progressive overload targets. Four training days per week; cardio 2–3 days per the cardio plan; HIIT day and plyometric/power day are integrated starting Week 4.

Week 4
